lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Edo, winter 1858.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Snow falls on a wooden bridge.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: You smell charcoal smoke.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your breath turns white.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: A shop sign catches your eye.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It says mountain whale.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Wait.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: There are no whales in the mountains.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's wild boar.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And that funny name is a cover story.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For more than a thousand years, Japan had mostly avoided beef and other farm animals.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The first ban came in 675.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And it had holes from day one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Yet today, Japan is famous for wagyu.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's some of the priciest beef on Earth.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So why did Japan avoid beef for about 1,200 years?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And how did it become the land of wagyu?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Here's the twist.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Japan never fully banned meat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It spent 1,200 years inventing loopholes.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It isn't one reason.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's six, all tangled together.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One starts in a muddy rice field, behind a patient ox.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Another is a polite thank-you letter.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About beef.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And one ends at the palace gate, with the Emperor himself.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Every reason is a piece of this puzzle.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: When all six fit, you'll have the answer.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The first piece is the oldest.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's a law, and it left the door open.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Japan, the year 675.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Emperor Tenmu sends out a new order.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: We can still read it in an old book, the Nihon Shoki.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The order is short.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Don't eat cows, horses, dogs, monkeys or chickens.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It also limits some hunting traps and fish traps.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But look at what's missing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Deer and wild boar aren't on the list.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And those were the wild meats people in Japan had eaten for ages.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The ban also seems tied to the farming months, roughly late spring to autumn.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians still argue whether it ran all year.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The old text can be read both ways.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So the law was strict about cows and horses, but quiet about deer and boar.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And Tenmu's order wasn't the last.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Later rulers kept giving similar orders for centuries.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So the law set a rule, with gaps built in.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece one: LAW.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But a law alone can't last 1,200 years.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For that, you need a rice field.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Imagine you're a rice farmer in the eighth century.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your whole year depends on this muddy field.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Plowing that mud by hand is brutal.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So you have help: a big, calm ox.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: If that ox could talk, he'd say: I pull the plow.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: I'm not lunch.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 741, Emperor Shomu repeated the rule in a new order.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: No killing cattle or horses.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: His reason was simple.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: These animals work in place of people.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Their work feeds people.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So a cow wasn't dinner.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It was your tractor.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And there's a second rice link.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Some people believed meat during rice season could ruin the harvest.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That may be why the old ban lined up with the growing months.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the strangest part is still ahead.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This rice logic lasted for centuries.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Jump to 1587.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The powerful ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi writes a memo.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Item eleven is blunt.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Buying, selling, killing or eating cattle and horses is wrong.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: More than nine hundred years after Tenmu, the cow was still a worker first.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece two: RICE.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The cow was simply too useful to eat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But usefulness doesn't explain one thing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Why did meat start to feel wrong?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Picture a temple.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Incense drifts past a wooden pagoda.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Emperor Tenmu was a strong supporter of Buddhism.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And Buddhism asks people not to kill living things.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Historians often link his order to the Buddhist idea of rebirth.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Lives come back again and again.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But there's a second thread.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It comes from Shinto, Japan's old local faith.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Shinto has an idea called kegare.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Basically, ritual impurity.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's not about being dirty.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Think of it as a state that keeps you away from sacred rituals.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In 927, a rulebook called the Engishiki spelled out the details.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Eat meat, and you had to stay away from shrine rituals for three days.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Three days.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's a long time-out for one bowl of stew.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And that feeling grew.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Over the centuries, meat slowly drifted off people's plates.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Sadly, the families who did butchering and leather work, in buraku communities, faced unfair treatment for centuries.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So faith and ritual turned an old rule into a deep habit.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece three: PURITY.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: We're halfway there, and the weirdest pieces are still coming.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But if people avoided meat, what kept them going?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The answer was all around them.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Japan is a chain of islands.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The sea is never far away.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the meat bans mostly left fish alone.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fish and rice stayed on the table.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So people still had protein.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That made the ban much easier to live with.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Here's how deep that habit runs.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In Japanese homes, meat only passed fresh fish in 2007.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's very recent history.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fish eating has dropped since its peak in 2001.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Back then, it was about 40 kilos a person.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Quick guess. How much beef does the average person in Japan eat each year?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One kilo, twenty-five kilos, or six? Take a guess.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About six kilos. That's roughly half a kilo a month.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So beef is still a small part of the plate.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Fish keeps a much bigger share.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: One quick thing.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Next week: why Europe was afraid of the potato.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Subscribe so it finds you.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The sea made the ban easy to keep.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece four: SEA.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But easy isn't the same as happy.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Some people still wanted meat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So they got creative.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Back to that snowy street in Edo.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Remember the mountain whale?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This is a real print by Hiroshige, from 1858.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Look at the left for that sign.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Shops like this had a clever excuse.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They called it kusurigui, which means medicine eating.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: You weren't eating meat for fun.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: No, this was for your health.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Wild boar even got a pretty nickname.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Botan, which means peony, the flower.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: If the boar could talk, he'd say: I'm a whale now.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Please don't ask.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: By the late Edo period, shops selling wild meat were doing well.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But the boldest loophole wasn't boar.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It was beef.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Meet Hikone, a castle town in what's now Shiga Prefecture.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The story goes that in 1687, a man here made beef pickled in miso.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He based it on a Chinese medicine book.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And he gave it a medicine name: henpongan.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In the 1780s, Hikone sent miso beef to the family of the shogun, Japan's military ruler.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Hikone is often called the only place allowed to make beef back then.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the next part sounds made up.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It isn't.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Imagine you're Tokugawa Nariaki, a powerful lord, in 1848.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Another gift of beef arrives from Hikone.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So you write a thank-you note to Hikone's lord.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Thank you for the beef you keep sending.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: I use it as medicine too.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So even top lords ate beef, as long as it was called medicine.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Meat never really vanished.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It just changed its name.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece five: LOOPHOLES.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But loopholes only work while the rule stands.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the rule was about to fall.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Look at this tiny island in Nagasaki harbor.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: It's called Dejima.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Dutch traders lived here.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And they kept cows, pigs and chickens.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: This print from 1861 shows foreigners from five nations at a banquet.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The meat-eaters had arrived.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And in 1862, Yokohama got its first gyunabe shop.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's beef simmered in a pot.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then came early 1872.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Emperor Meiji lifted the old ban on meat.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the court let it be known that he would eat meat himself.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: His reason wasn't mainly health.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: He told an advisor meat mattered more for dealing with foreigners.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Not everyone agreed.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About a month later, ten mountain ascetics in white tried to force their way into the palace.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Ascetics are people who give up comforts for their faith.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: These men followed a faith centered on Mount Ontake.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They believed foreign ways were making the land impure.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The guards stopped them, and four of the men died.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For them, this was about faith, not food.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: But in the cities, beef caught on fast.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People sat cross-legged around steaming pots.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Kanagaki Robun even wrote a book about it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Its name means cross-legged at the beef pot.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Your turn. By 1877, how many beef pot shops were there in Tokyo?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: About 50, over 550, or about 5,000? Take a guess.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Over 550. And that's just five years after the ban ended.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Now look at Tokyo's cattle for beef over thirty years.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: The number grew more than seven times.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: With the emperor on board, city menus changed within decades.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That's piece six: EMPEROR.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And the puzzle is complete.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So, remember that shop sign in the snow?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: That funny name was a loophole.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Here's the whole answer.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Law, rice and purity rules pushed beef away, and the sea made that easy.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Loopholes kept meat alive, until an emperor ended the ban.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And here's the last twist.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Kobe beef, a famous kind of wagyu, comes from Tajima cattle.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: For a long time, those cattle weren't food.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: They were work animals that pulled plows.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Then Kobe's port opened in 1868, and foreigners started eating them.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Today, Kobe beef is some of the most expensive beef in the world.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: From plow to plate.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Still, the sea never lost.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: People in Japan eat about six kilos of beef a year.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: And about 21 kilos of fish.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: In the land of wagyu, fish still wins, more than three to one.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: So that's how a country that avoided beef ended up famous for it.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Next week, a whole continent gets scared of a vegetable.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Why was Europe afraid of the potato?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Subscribe so it finds you.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: Until then, tell me one thing in the comments.

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: What food would you call medicine, just so you could eat it?

lines.speaker: kaxo
lines.text: See you next week.
